summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply of their own force: the Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council, and no such extension appears in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap facing a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker.

Statutory discrimination protection covering gender reassignment has been in place since the Equal Opportunities Act 2006 took effect on 1 March 2007. The Act prohibits discrimination in employment and in the provision of goods and services on the ground of gender reassignment, defined as a process for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex. Sexual orientation is a protected ground under the same Act.

Hate-crime coverage extends to trans people. Parliament amended the Crimes Act 2011 in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, with approval on 19 September, royal assent on 25 September and effect from 10 October 2013. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity.

In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would urgently consider legislation to tackle what the Chief Minister, Fabian Picardo, called "disgusting lurking homophobia" on social media during Pride month, following an incident of anti-gay abuse. The proposal at that stage concerned sexual orientation; the trans-inclusive amendment came in July 2026.

In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy. The sourced excerpt states the offence generally without specifying whether its scope covers sexual orientation, transgender identity, or both.

Partner recognition is established locally. Civil partnerships have been available since March 2014, and same-sex marriage since 15 December 2016, after the Civil Marriage Amendment Act passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, received royal assent on 1 November and took effect on 15 December, with the first marriage the following day. A deputy registrar may opt out, requiring assignment of an alternative registrar. Because no gender-recognition route exists, a trans visitor's legal sex for marriage purposes remains that recorded at birth; a relationship locally read as same-sex can be registered.

Adoption is open to same-sex couples. The Supreme Court ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, and the Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024, expressly allowing same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

The age of consent is 16 for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the previous age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012.
tangentialFactors:
The House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 inquiry into the overseas territories recommended that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status be made illegal in all overseas territories, and its Seventh Report of 2007-08 sets accountability and good-governance expectations applicable to Gibraltar.

Male same-sex sexual activity defined legally as male sodomy was decriminalised in Gibraltar in 1993 following pressure from the European Court of Human Rights and the Government of the United Kingdom; the Victorian-drafted law addressed only men, so no equivalent provision applied to women.

A private member's bill to equalise the age of consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009, two years before the Supreme Court ruled the higher age unconstitutional.

The 2006 Constitution does not mention sexual orientation; proposals in 2002 omitted it.

The 2016 marriage reform followed a December 2015 consultation that left Gibraltarians polarized. A government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints, and the main parties indicated support for the change.
localsOnly:
Civil partnerships, available since March 2014, grant most rights of marriage including adoption, as mandated by the Supreme Court's 2013 ruling. Where a deputy registrar opts out of conducting a marriage, an alternative registrar must be assigned.

In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority amended its in vitro fertilisation policy to allow lesbian couples access to assisted reproductive technology. In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for individuals and for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination.

Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 or the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 has been extended to Gibraltar by Order in Council is not established in the sourced material.

The July 2026 conversion therapy offence is stated generally; whether its scope covers sexual orientation, transgender identity, or both is not specified in the sourced material.

No enforcement data on the 2013 or 2026 hate-crime provisions appears in the inventory, so the practical operation of the transgender-identity amendment is not sourced.

The July 2021 statement that the Ministry for Justice and Equality would urgently consider further legislation is not sourced to an enacted outcome other than the July 2026 amendments.
